summary:
Development of a wildfire prediction system based on satellite data and imagery, using Deep Learning. The system uses NASA FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS) and Google Earth Engine FIRMS, and ConvLSTM neural networks to model spatio-temporal fire dynamics. It uses, as input, satellite data from the previous 30 days to predict, as output, fire occurrences for the following 30 days, divided into 6 consecutive 5-day intervals.
Region of INterest : Madagascar

It addresses the challenge of predicting wildfire occurrences in Madagascar, where the vast geographical coverage and limited accessibility of remote areas make early detection particularly difficult
details:
The project develops an end-to-end wildfire prediction system that processes satellite observations.

The data pipeline combines NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS) with satellite imagery accessed through Google Earth Engine. For the prediction model, We focused on the T21 brightness-temperature band, transforming satellite observations into grayscale images.

The prediction approach uses a ConvLSTM (Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory) architecture, which combines convolutional operations for spatial feature extraction with recurrent mechanisms for learning temporal dependencies. The model receives 6 consecutive 5-day satellite images, covering the previous 30 days, and predicts fire occurrence for the next 30 days, also represented by 6 5-day intervals.

This is particularly relevant to Madagascar, where wildfires threaten forests, agricultural resources, and local communities.

The project was developed using:

  • PythoN : Main programming language for data processing, model development, and backend implementation.
  • NASA FIRMS (MODIS/VIIRS): Satellite-based fire detection observations.
  • Google Earth Engine FIRMS: Satellite imagery access and processing.
  • TensorFlow / Keras: Deep learning framework used to develop and train the ConvLSTM architecture.
  • Gradio: Development of the user interface.
  • Prefect Cloud: Data pipeline orchestration and workflow management.
  • Hugging Face: Hosting datasets, trained models, and the application.
  • Google Colab: GPU/TPU-accelerated model training and experimentation.

The main considerations included:

  • Data availability: Relying on accessible satellite datasets covering Madagascar over multiple years.
  • Computational constraints: Selecting an architecture that could be developed using available computing resources.
  • Temporal resolution: Using five-day intervals to represent the evolution of fire activity.
